title: Mirabai
hook: a princess ties bells to her ankles and dances in public, and people call her mad

segments.voice: Yesterday, Andal's dream of a wedding, a thousand elephants and a bride who walked into the shrine. Did you tell one quiet hope to someone? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-six.

Small brass bells, strung on a cord and tied around the ankles. Every step rings. You can't sneak anywhere wearing them; that's rather the point. Dancers wear them on stage. In one of the songs sung in her name, a princess ties them on and dances, in public, for Krishna. The town talks. Her husband's family is mortified. And the song doesn't hide any of it. It repeats what people said about her, and then it shrugs. Year three heard Mira's poison cup and her treasure. Today, her feet.
screen: `BELLS TIED AROUND THE ANKLES.` → `THE TOWN TALKS.` → `TODAY, HER FEET.`

segments.voice: The song opens with the line people know it by, pag ghunghroo bandh Mira nachi re. Here's the sense of it, in paraphrase. Mira tied bells on her feet and danced. I've made myself my Lord's own servant. People say Mira's gone mad. My mother-in-law says I've ruined the family. And the last line: Mira's Lord is Giridhar, and she has met the undying one with ease. First, look at who's speaking about her. The people, the mother-in-law, the family: the song lets them all have their say. It doesn't argue back. It just goes on dancing. The mother-in-law's word, ruin of the family, shows the line a royal woman crossed by dancing in the open. The song knows that, and names it. Second, the word for mad there is bawari, and in Mira's songs madness isn't only an insult. In another song she calls herself prem diwani, mad with love. So the charge the town throws at her becomes something she wears, the way she wears the bells. Third, the bells make devotion something you can hear. Bhakti, the way of loving devotion, isn't only a feeling in the chest. In Mira's songs it moves the feet, keeps a rhythm, gathers a crowd. These songs are still sung with a drum and cymbals, in temples and living rooms, and sometimes danced. A song about a woman who wouldn't keep still is very hard to sing sitting still.
screen: `MIRA TIED BELLS ON HER FEET` · `THE TOWN HAS ITS SAY` · `MAD, THE WORD SHE WEARS` · `DEVOTION YOU CAN HEAR`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: rhythm in the body. Sit comfortably and find the breath. Now, very softly, let one hand tap your knee, slowly, in time with the breath. In, one tap. Out, one tap. Feel how the rhythm steadies you. After a few rounds, let the hand rest and keep the beat inside, just in the breath. If you pray, you can let the name you love ride that rhythm. The bell holds the time.
Mirabai. In one of her songs she ties bells on her ankles and dances for Krishna, and when the town calls her mad, she takes the word as her own. Today's word.
Your line: Mirabai. Today, let some music move you, even just a foot tapping under the table, and notice what that does. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-six.

howItsDone: Mira's songs are sung as bhajans, with drums and cymbals, in temples, homes and concert halls, and some are danced in classical and folk styles.

original.note: Hindi. -bai is a respectful ending for a woman's name in western India; the songs mostly call her simply Mira.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mira was a quiet saint, praying alone.
what it means: in her songs she dances in public, ankle bells ringing, while the town talks.
what a scholar hears: the town calls her bawari, mad, and in another song she calls herself prem diwani, mad with love.
